title: IB Maths AA Extended Response: Plan, Write, Check
summary: IB Maths AA extended response tips: decode questions, plan in two minutes, show clear working, and check your reasoning to earn marks under exam pressure.
body_markdown:
An **IB Maths AA extended response** becomes more manageable when you turn it into a sequence: decode the instructions, map the connected parts, write a visible mathematical argument, and check that your conclusion answers the question. Under time pressure, the aim is to make each useful step clear enough to earn credit.


Imagine reaching a longer question and recognising the topic, but not the route. Your instinct might be to start calculating immediately. A brief pause can save you from solving the wrong problem beautifully.


The routine below helps you use that pause well, then turn your working into a response an examiner can follow.


### Your extended-response checklist


Before you begin, establish five things:


- **The destination:** What must you find, show, explain, or justify?
- **The restrictions:** What domain, interval, accuracy, or contextual conditions apply?
- **The connections:** Which earlier results could help later parts?
- **The method:** Which equation, theorem, representation, or calculator operation fits?
- **The evidence:** What working will explain how you reached your answer?


Keep this checklist beside you while practising with the[IB Maths AA Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-math-aa/questionbank) . Eventually, the questions become habits.


### Decode the question before doing the mathematics


Read the whole question once, including the final part. A long response often develops one mathematical situation through several connected steps. Seeing the destination can explain why the opening parts matter.


Then underline the command terms. “Find” asks for an answer supported by appropriate working. “Show that” supplies the destination, so your task is to establish it through valid reasoning. “Hence” signals that an earlier result should inform your next step.


Pay equal attention to small restrictions. A solution outside the stated domain may be mathematically valid but irrelevant. An exact answer and a decimal approximation are different requests. A stationary point and a maximum are different conclusions.


Translate the wording into a short task statement: “Differentiate, find candidates, classify them, then compare endpoint values.” That sentence gives your working direction.


For more practice recognising these connections, use the[guide to answering long IB Maths AA questions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-maths-aa-how-to-answer-long-questions) .


### Plan in two minutes, then start


Treat two minutes as a planning ceiling for a substantial question, not a compulsory delay. A shorter question may need only a few seconds.


### First minute: map the route


Beside each part, jot the likely operation: substitute, differentiate, solve, integrate, interpret. Draw a small arrow where one answer feeds into another.


Identify any part you can attempt independently. Getting stuck on an early calculation does not automatically prevent you from making progress later.


### Second minute: choose the first useful line


Write the equation or relationship that starts the solution. For an optimisation problem, this might be a model for the quantity being maximised. For probability, it might be a distribution statement or conditional probability expression.


Also check the question's mark allocation. Use it as a clue to the expected depth of working, while budgeting time across the whole paper. Avoid spending several minutes repeatedly trying the same unsuccessful manipulation.


A student asks a calculator wearing a wizard hat to solve time management, and the calculator suggests starting.

Notice what makes this complete. The working identifies candidates, checks the interval boundaries, and distinguishes the greatest value from the locations where it occurs.


For an **IB Maths AA long answer** , short connecting phrases such as “setting the derivative equal to zero” or “comparing endpoint values” make your reasoning easier to follow. You rarely need lengthy prose.


### Make calculator work explainable


On a calculator-permitted paper, show what you asked the calculator to do. Write the equation being solved, the integral being evaluated, or the probability being calculated before recording its output.


For a numerical solution, include any relevant interval or restriction. For a graph-based argument, label the features that support your conclusion. A number by itself can leave the method unclear.


Keep sufficient precision during intermediate calculations, then apply the requested accuracy to your final answer. Check angle settings when trigonometry is involved.


The[IB Maths AA Paper 2 preparation guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-to-expect-in-ib-math-aa-paper-2-a-student-guide-to-scoring-smart) offers a useful next step for practising calculator decisions alongside mathematical working.


### Check your response against the mark scheme


During the exam, you cannot see the mark scheme. You can still inspect your answer for the evidence it is likely to require:


- Have I shown the method rather than only the result?
- Have I justified any requested conclusion?
- Have I answered every part, including units and restrictions?
- Does the result make sense when substituted or estimated?


During practice, compare your response with the actual mark scheme. IB Mathematics mark schemes distinguish method and accuracy credit, and follow-through credit can apply when an earlier incorrect result is used correctly later. Its availability depends on the question and marking instructions, so clear working matters.


Label each lost mark by its cause: misunderstanding, method selection, algebra, calculator use, or communication. Then redo the relevant part without looking at the solution. The[Maths AA last-minute revision guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-maths-aa-last-minute-revision-priorities) can help you prioritise recurring weaknesses.


### Build the routine before the next timed paper


If you search for **IB Maths AA essay technique** , focus on mathematical communication: a logical sequence, justified steps, and a precise conclusion. The response should be as long as the reasoning requires.


RevisionDojo brings that preparation together. Use Study Notes to repair a concept, Flashcards to revisit conditions and definitions, and AI Chat to explore a confusing step. Grading tools can support feedback, while Tutors offer another route when a difficulty persists. The Coursework Library serves a separate purpose when your attention turns to mathematical exploration.


Start with one longer response in the Questionbank. Review it carefully, then sit timed papers in **Exam mode** , using Mock Exams or Predicted Papers as practice material where available. Treat predicted material as preparation, never a forecast of what will appear.


The goal is to make good decisions familiar before the clock starts. Build that routine through[RevisionDojo's IB Maths AA resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-math-aa) , one clearly reasoned response at a time.
